title: John Mearsheimer: Israel-Palestine, Russia-Ukraine, China, NATO, and WW3 | Lex Fridman Podcast #401
summary: A realist scholar argues NATO expansion caused the Ukraine war, nuclear weapons make great-power war unlikely but escalation is unknowable, and a US-China war is possible but avoidable.

assertions.quote: what they were negotiating about was NATO expansion into Ukraine, which was the principle cause of the war
There's no evidence he was interested in conquering all of Ukraine.

verdicts.note: A leader's private aims cannot be shown from the public record; the initial force was small for occupation, yet the drive on Kyiv suggests regime change was sought.

assertions.quote: The answer is the United States and Britain get involved and tell Zelensky to walk.

verdicts.note: Western leaders discouraged the Istanbul framework, but the talks also foundered on security guarantees and the Bucha revelations; Western veto as the decisive cause is disputed.

assertions.quote: if Russia were losing in Ukraine, that's the one scenario where I think where Russia would've used nuclear weapons.

verdicts.note: Russian doctrine allows first use when the state is threatened and US officials feared it in late 2022, but Russia absorbed the Kharkiv and Kherson defeats without nuclear use.

assertions.quote: Well, once you do that, you have a great power war. You have NATO versus Russia

verdicts.note: US officials publicly threatened catastrophic conventional consequences for Russian nuclear use, a path that could bring NATO and Russia into direct combat, though it is only a possibility.
RAND lists the 'possibility of NATO entry into the war' as a main factor restraining Russian nuclear use inside Ukraine, i.e. both sides see a nuclear strike as able to pull NATO in.

assertions.quote: There's no question that the presence of nuclear weapons, makes it much less likely.
And this supports your basic point that bad things happen.
this economic prosperity is unable to prevent World War I, because security concerns or survival is more important.
there is a real possibility of war. Whether or not we avoid it is very hard to say.

verdicts.note: Forecasters put a US-China war in the coming years well under even odds but not negligible, consistent with a real but avoidable risk.
Forecasters put a US-China war at 8.7% before 2035 and 25% before 2050: a real possibility that is more likely than not to be avoided.
CSIS: 'A war over Taiwan is not certain, but it is not unimaginable either'; it argues deterrence is achievable but does not draw the Cold War comparison.

The case file calls the US-Soviet Cold War one of history's greatest escapes from the trap: despite close calls and proxy wars the two militaries never fought directly, through nuclear fear, mutual limits on competition and arms-control cooperation. That is a precedent for avoiding war, not proof that a US-China war can be avoided.

Hanania lays out two ways to avoid a US-China war: manage China's challenge, or have no challenge at all if China rises like postwar Japan or the US stops holding its military position in East Asia. On this view war is avoidable and a matter of choice.

assertions.quote: It is very, very hard to attack across a body of water.

verdicts.note: Military analysts and wargames agree a contested amphibious crossing of about 100 miles is among the hardest operations, one reason most expect blockade or coercion before invasion.

assertions.quote: I think it's probably not even possible now to beat the Chinese in a war over Taiwan

verdicts.note: Public wargames such as CSIS's 2023 series found a Chinese invasion usually fails against a US, Taiwan and Japan defence, though at very heavy cost to all.

CSIS's wargame found the US and Taiwan 'could successfully defend the island even under relatively pessimistic assumptions', contrary to many observers' impressions, though only if four conditions hold.

assertions.quote: Putin has, on more than one occasion, very subtly rattled the nuclear sword.

verdicts.note: Russian officials repeatedly issued nuclear warnings tied to Western aid, and Western governments cited escalation fears when delaying some weapons, though support kept growing.
